dialogue.agent: Hello, how may I help you today?

dialogue.user: Hi! I'm looking for a book that gives good advice—maybe something in self-help or personal growth. My budget is around $15 to $30. Also, I only want books that are really highly rated. Do you have anything you can recommend?
dialogue.agent:
Here are three highly rated options in the self-help/personal growth category within your $15–$30 budget:

- **Where Women Have No Doctor: A Health Guide for Women** ($26.95, 4.6 stars from 16 reviews): Combines self-help medical advice with a focus on how poverty and culture affect women's health worldwide. Developed by medical experts from over 30 countries.

- **The Covenant with Black America** ($15.76, 4.5 stars from 48 reviews): A collection of essays tackling critical social issues, offering practical advice for personal and community growth, with contributions from Tavis Smiley, Cornel West, and others.

- **Go Love Yourself: The Ultimate Guide to #liveyourbestlife** ($26.99, 4.4 stars from 1 review): Offers guidance for personal growth and self-love.

Would you like more details or customer reviews for any of these?

products.title: Where Women Have No Doctor: A Health Guide for Women
products.description: From the Back Cover Where Women Have No Doctor combines self-help medical information with an understanding of the ways poverty, discrimination and cultural beliefs limit women's health and access to care. Developed with community-based groups and medical experts from more than 30 countries, this book can help anyone understand, treat and prevent many of the health problems that affect women.

products.title: The Covenant with Black America
products.description: From Booklist This collection of essays is both a plea and a response to the self-assessed critical circumstances of black America today. Tavis Smiley provides the introduction, touching on the issues he explores as host and interviewer on public television and radio; Cornel West and Haki Madhubuti also provide commentary, tying together the common theme of planning how to address the circumstances faced by black Americans. Marian Wright Edelman offers the statement of purpose introducing the 10 covenants, pledging individual effort in the areas of health care, public education, criminal justice, community-centered policing, affordable neighborhoods, democracy, agriculture, economics, environmental justice, and technology. Among the contributors are Marc H. Morial, Angela Glover Blackwell, and Wade Henderson. Each section offers facts on racial disparities in the U.S.; practical suggestions on what individuals, communities, and the government can do to rectify problems; and other helpful resources. Although specifically aimed at problems and issues facing black America, this work has appeal for all readers interested in social issues that plague the nation as a whole. Vernon Ford Copyright © American Library Association. All rights reserved About the Author Tavis Smiley is the author of eight books, including ""Doing What's Right, Hard Left, How to Make Black America Better, ""and ""Keeping the Faith."" He hosts an eponymous talk and interview show

dialogue.user: Thanks! Could you share some customer review excerpts—especially about the advice in "Where Women Have No Doctor: A Health Guide for Women"? I’m curious how readers felt about its practical tips and usefulness.
dialogue.agent:
Here are excerpts from readers of **Where Women Have No Doctor: A Health Guide for Women** about its practical advice:

- “So full of information and health tips. The author included when to transport for medical attention, leaving everything clear including when NOT to self-treat, when and what situations are emergencies, and how to do correct self-care. A lot of little things one might not consider or think about.” (5 stars)

- “Great book! Highly recommend it! I particularly like that it is written in simple, easy-to-understand terms with illustrations. It provides basic but key information about women's health care.” (5 stars)

- “All of the ‘what to do’ sections read ‘seek medical attention.’ The title of the book is ‘Where Women Have No Doctor’!! … it gives some basic advice but that’s about it.” (1 star)

Most readers found the advice practical and accessible, though one reviewer felt there could be more detail for situations where medical attention isn’t available. Would you like further details or info about another title?

dialogue.user: Thank you for sharing those reviews—they’re really helpful! For the positive reviews, it sounds like there’s a lot of clear, actionable advice, which is great. I am curious, though: does "Where Women Have No Doctor: A Health Guide for Women" cover general life advice too, or is it mainly focused on health? And do you have any books with a perfect 5-star average rating that fit my budget and advice-related interests?
dialogue.agent:
"Where Women Have No Doctor: A Health Guide for Women" is primarily focused on women's health—covering prevention, self-care, reproductive health, mental health, and related challenges impacted by social factors. It includes some life advice (like dealing with discrimination and violence) but centers on health and wellness rather than general life philosophy or broad self-help topics.

If you’re looking for a highly rated, advice-oriented book with a perfect 5-star average in your budget, consider **Notes To A Five-Year-Old** ($15.65, 5.0 stars from 1 review). It’s a collection of essays, observations, and heartfelt advice written by a father to his young daughter. Reviewers describe it as thoughtful, perceptive, and deeply moving, with relatable wisdom for both parents and anyone reflecting on childhood or family life.

Would you like a brief excerpt or more details about "Notes To A Five-Year-Old"?

result.title: Where Women Have No Doctor: A Health Guide for Women
result.features: This 2020 updated printing features updated antiretroviral information based on new World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines to treat HIV and prevent mother-to-child transmission. Other updated topics include: treatment of sexually transmitted infections (STI's); family planning; cervical, breast and other cancers; eclampsia; care for women who have had abortions; and medicines. All Hesperian books are regularly updated and reprinted to reflect accurate medical information. Where Women Have No Doctor has been written to help women care for their own health, and to help community health workers or others to meet women's health needs problems that affect specifically women, or that affect women in different ways from men. It combines self-help medical information with an understanding of the ways in which poverty, discrimination and cultural beliefs may limit women's health or access to care. Developed with community-based groups and medical experts from more than 30 countries, this book aims to help anyone understand, treat and prevent many of the health problems that can affect women. Topics featured in the book include: how to solve health problems; ways to stay healthy; understanding the reproductive parts of women's bodies; sexual health; HIV/AIDS and other sexually transmitted diseases; pregnancy, birth and breast feeding; mental health; health concerns of women with disabilities, girls, older women and refugees; the politics of women's health; rape and other violence against women; and the use of medicines in women's health.

Developed with community-based groups and medical experts from more than 30 countries, this book can help anyone understand, treat and prevent many of the health problems that affect women.

products.title: Notes To A Five-Year-Old
products.description: Review "Notes To a Five-Year-Old is a book that I could not put down until I was finished. I was completely and totally captivated. I cried on almost every page.  I think that this is a book that all parents can relate to. I think all children, which is all of us, can respond to deeply." Pamela Eakins, PhD Author of The American Way of Birth"Notes To a Five-Year-Old is a thoughtful and perceptive view of the forgotten world of childhood as seen through the eyes of a wise and observant father...a poignant and humorous map of the unfathomable depths of the five-year-old mind ...and the magical world of children."Richard J. Correlli, MDPsychiatrist, Stanford University About the Author Bill Morris is a San Francisco Bay Area writer and author of twelve books. One of Bill's books of which he is most proud is Notes To a Five-Year-Old, a group of essays, fatherly observations, and advice written for his daughter when she was five. He has also published two additional books of family essays, The Red Jacket, essays for his daughter about her mother who was lost to cancer, and Good Morning, Ryan, a book of humor, insights, and vignettes of childhood for his second five-year-old daughter, Ryan Rosemary. His latest book, The Astral Zoo, is a novel that describes the life of zoo animals who live in freedom in the zoo as astral beings, living as animals struggling for meaning in a potentially meaningless place. Bill has published many magazine articles and written as a software columnist for the San Francisco Chronicle. His books are mainly in the computer field and he's been an acquisitions editor with Hayden Book Company, a trade computer book publisher. His first novel, Grey Goddess, about California mysticism, surfing, and the search for lost spirit, received excellent reviews and praise around the world. Surfing magazine said, "A true but comical depiction of the surfing lifestyle, Bill Morris has hit the lip with his book Grey Goddess!" Grey Goddess has sold in surfing and water-related sports stores throughout the United States and abroad. Reviewers have compared it to Way of the Peaceful Warrior, Golf in the Kingdom, and even Siddartha.

Here’s an excerpt from a customer about the advice in **Notes To A Five-Year-Old**:

“When I was five years old I lost my mother and life changed. This book was like her talking to me and offering me guidance. It really spoke to my heart and soul. If your inner child needs this voice, I suggest you read!”

The review highlights the book’s nurturing, heartfelt guidance—aimed at both comforting and providing life perspective for readers of any age. Would you like to move forward with this choice, or do you want more options?
